1|# Review: task 4 Oz pipeline
2|
3|Verdict: approve with fixes. No blocker. Fix findings 1 and 2 before any app code reads these data files; fix 3 to 5 before the soundtrack step runs for real.
4|
5|What this change does: ingests the Oz text into `book.json`, splits chapters into scenes with Meta, classifies each scene with Jev plus a Meta override on low confidence, and clusters scene vectors into 15 track prompts. New code in `core/` and `pipeline/`, committed data in `data/books/oz/`, with tests beside each module.
6|
7|## Findings
8|
9|1. **Stored Jev fields use camelCase against the snake_case spec** (should-fix), `core/types.ts:59-70`, `data/books/oz/analysis.json`.
10|   Problem: the spec asked for `intensity_confidence` and `tempo_confidence`, but the stored scenes carry `intensityConfidence`, `tempoConfidence`, `inputTokens`, `outputTokens`, while provenance in the same file uses `prompt_tokens` and `cached_tokens`. One file mixes two conventions.
11|   Fix: rename the stored Jev fields to snake_case in `JevResult`, update the two readers (`pipeline/classify.ts`, `pipeline/jev.ts`), and rewrite `analysis.json` from the next classify run.
12|
13|2. **Sad and dark clusters never get the minor-key variant** (should-fix), `core/music-prompt.ts:6-7, 32-44`.
14|   Problem: the spec asked for minor variants for sad or dark moods, but the base hardcodes "in a major key" and `buildTrackPrompt` has no mood branch. The grief cluster (t05, tristeza 0.86) and the dread cluster (t08, suspenso/tristeza) both ship major-key prompts.
15|   Fix: switch the base to a minor-key leitmotif when the top mood is tristeza, suspenso, or misterio, and keep major otherwise. One branch, no new module.
16|
17|3. **Two cluster pairs yield near-identical prompts** (should-fix), `data/books/oz/music-clusters.json` t12/t13 and t14/t15.
18|   Problem: t12 and t13 carry the same mood text ("driving and fierce, tense and expectant") with the same dynamics and differ only in BPM; t14 and t15 use the same two mood words in swapped order. Fixed k=15 splits tiny groups (t08 and t12 hold 2 scenes each), and the prompt template has too few degrees of freedom to tell them apart.
19|   Fix: after sorting, merge clusters whose top-two moods match and whose BPM ranges overlap, or widen the template (dynamics, register) so centroids this close still read differently.
20|
21|4. **Dynamics buckets call fight scenes "moderate"** (should-fix), `core/music-prompt.ts:26-30`.
22|   Problem: three coarse buckets put intensity 0.49 (t12), 0.54 (t13), and 0.63 (t08) all under "moderate dynamics". The fiercest scenes in the book get the same dynamics word as a calm river rest.
23|   Fix: cut the top bucket at 0.5 instead of 0.67, or word dynamics from the dominant emotion as well as intensity.
24|
25|5. **Meta retries stack three deep** (should-fix), `pipeline/meta.ts:42-52`, `pipeline/segment.ts:90`.
26|   Problem: `completeJson` loops 3 attempts around `fetchWithRetry` with `attempts: 3`, so one call can fire up to 9 requests; the segment validation retry doubles that to 18 per chapter. The spec asked for 3 attempts with backoff plus one retry on invalid output.
27|   Fix: keep one loop. Drop the outer for-loop in `completeJson` and let `fetchWithRetry` own network retries; keep the single validation retry in segment.
28|
29|6. **Unused error parameter in the retry check** (nit), `pipeline/http.ts:8`.
30|   Problem: `isRetryable(status, _error)` takes an argument it never reads, so future callers will guess what it is for.
31|   Fix: delete the parameter and update the two call sites.
32|
33|7. **Cluster scene lookup is quadratic** (nit), `pipeline/cluster-tracks.ts:39-43`.
34|   Problem: `classified.find` runs per point per cluster. At 133 scenes this is instant, but it is a needless nested scan.
35|   Fix: build one `Map` from scene id to scene before the cluster loop.
36|
37|## Checked and fine
38|
39|- Core purity: no `process.env`, `node:` imports, `fetch`, or `fs` in `core/`. Secrets stay in env, read only in `pipeline/build.ts`. Errors carry status plus a short body excerpt; no headers or keys are logged. No MusicGen, Modal, or audio code anywhere.
40|- Scene coverage (recomputed on the committed files): 24 chapters, 1104 paragraphs with sequential `n`, 133 scenes, 0 gaps, 0 overlaps, 0 chapter crossings. All range logic compares `n`.
41|- Failure handling: 0 hard failures, 0 null finals, `unclustered` empty. Every final vector sums to 1. Every override vector holds exactly the 8 ids. The override rate is 33.8% (45 of 133), all from genuine low confidence or `unknown`-max cases in the spot check.
42|- Scene plausibility: the cyclone reads tristeza, suspenso, asombro, then calma, in order. The poppy Meadow reads calm and bright before the sleep scene turns to suspenso. The Winged Monkeys arc moves from lost (tristeza/aventura tie) to summoning (aventura/asombro) to arrival (alegria). The Kalidah attack fits except for one soft edge: the book's clearest fight scene lands suspenso 0.83 with combate only 0.16, so the energy sits in intensity 0.72 and tempo 0.89 rather than in the vector.
43|- Tests prove behavior: `npm test` passes 31/31, including override, hard-failure-stores-no-vector, determinism, and the committed-data test. `npm run typecheck` is clean. Cost math matches the spec rates by hand: Jev 134284 input tokens at 0.042 per 1M gives $0.0056; Meta 86521 prompt with 11025 cached plus 60080 completion at 0.10/0.002/0.20 gives $0.0196; total $0.0252, under the $0.10 budget.
44|- Config: only the four allowed devDependencies, scripts match the spec, size ignore plus test cover `data/books/`, hook tests pass 40/40, secret scan exits 0, size check passes.
45|

47|
48|- The `typescript-best-practices` skill is disabled in this session, so TypeScript points rest on the typecheck run and reading, not on the skill. Live Jev and Meta response drift was not re-tested; the run provenance (133 Jev requests, 69 Meta requests) was read, not replayed.

2|
3|## Report a vulnerability
4|
5|Use GitHub private vulnerability reporting on this repo. Do not open a public issue for a security bug.
6|
7|## What is in place now
8|
9|- Secrets live only in env vars. `.env.example` holds names, never values.
10|- A pre-commit scan blocks staged secrets: gitleaks when installed, plus the built-in scanner in `scripts/check-secrets.mjs`, which always runs.
11|- Scans cover all tracked paths except lockfiles, including `agent-logs/`, `public/`, and `.agents/skills/`. CI runs the built-in scanner with `--all` plus pinned gitleaks v8.28.0 with a hardcoded sha256, and GitHub Actions pinned to commit SHAs.
12|- `.gitleaks.toml` extends the default gitleaks config and allowlists only the known test placeholder strings, never paths.
13|- GitHub secret scanning and push protection guard the remote.
14|- Dependabot alerts track vulnerable dependencies.
15|
16|## Rules for later tasks
17|
18|Planned, not built yet. Each app task implements its share.
19|
20|- The BYOK Meta key is never stored server-side or in logs. It stays in the browser session (`sessionStorage`) and travels over HTTPS per request in a header.
21|- The owner `META_API_KEY` funds the public chat and images within the per-person quota and the global cap. Once a person's quota is used, they may bring their own key (BYOK). A BYOK request uses only the user's key and never falls back to the owner key.
22|- BYOK requests are still rate-limited per IP.
23|- Logged error objects hold no keys, tokens, or raw provider output.
24|- HMAC comparisons run in constant time.
25|- The CSP allows `challenges.cloudflare.com` for scripts and frames, and `*.public.blob.vercel-storage.com` for images.
26|- Modal endpoints require proxy auth. Proxy tokens live only in env and travel as Modal-Key / Modal-Secret headers.

30|- Quotas are strict per person: 15 questions and 5 images per day, counted by hashed IP and anonymous cookie, whichever runs out first. A global spend cap in Redis sits above them.

1|Ponytail ruleset by DietrichGebert, MIT, github.com/DietrichGebert/ponytail (commit 09c434a). Level: full.

3|# Ponytail
4|
5|You are a lazy senior developer. The best code is the code never written. You solve the whole problem with the least new code. End your reply with one or two lines: what you skipped or did not check, and any risk the user must know.
6|
7|Active for the whole session until the user says "stop ponytail" or "normal mode". Switch level: `/ponytail lite|full|ultra`.
8|
9|## Before you write
10|
11|Read the task and the code it touches. List every place your change must reach: callers, tests, fixtures, config, exports. Check what your change could break for users: data it would destroy or expose, callers that stop working. That is scope. Extra features are not.
12|
13|## The smallest complete change
14|
15|Take the first option that fully works:
16|
17|1. Does it need to exist? Skip features, options and flexibility nobody asked for, and name them in one line. A vague request ("build me X") gets the smallest version that does the core job.
18|2. Already in this codebase (a helper, component, service, pattern)? Use it the way the surrounding code does.
19|3. Standard library or a platform feature? Use it, unless the project has its own. A house component beats a native widget.
20|4. An installed dependency? Use it. Never add a dependency for a few lines.
21|5. Can it be one line a reader gets at a glance? One line.
22|6. Otherwise: the minimum code that works.
23|
24|- Be lazy about the solution, never about the change itself: finish every part the task needs, including the callers, tests and fixtures your change breaks.
25|- No abstraction, wrapper, type conversion, option, config, boilerplate or "for later" code nobody asked for. Keep values in the form the platform already gives you. Deletion beats addition. Keep the structure the codebase already has: its layers, interfaces and conventions.
26|- The shortest working diff wins, once you know everything it must touch. A one-liner that needs decoding is not short.
27|- Comment only the why the code cannot show, in one line.
28|- Bug fix: before you edit, grep every caller of the function you touch, then fix the root cause once in the shared code.
29|- Code you move or merge keeps its error handling and validation.
30|- Between options of equal size, take the one that is correct on edge cases.
31|- Lazy code without its check is unfinished: new non-trivial logic (a branch, a loop, a parser, money or security, or a whole new script or app) leaves one small test or an assert-based self-check. Trivial changes need none.
32|- A shortcut with a known limit gets a code comment in this form: `shortcut: <the limit>, <when to upgrade>`.
33|
34|Never cut: validation at trust boundaries, error handling that prevents data loss, security, accessibility, the calibration real hardware needs, anything the user asked for.
35|
36|## Levels
37|
38|| Level | Behavior |
39||-------|----------|
40|| **lite** | Build what was asked. Name the smaller option in one line and let the user pick. |
41|| **full** | The rules above. Default. |
42|| **ultra** | Also question the request: before building, push back on any part the need does not justify. |
43|
44|Run `ponytail-review` on your own diff before you hand it back.
45|
46|## Skills
47|
48|All pstack and ponytail skills live in `.agents/skills/`. Muse Code loads them when the workspace starts with `--trust-workspace`. Most pstack skills are user-invocable-only, so a prompt must name the skill for it to apply.

51||-----------|-------|
52|| Designing a task | `architect` |
53|| Before writing logic | `principle-foundational-thinking`, `principle-type-system-discipline` |
54|| Writing TypeScript | `typescript-best-practices` |
55|| A bug with a cheap test | `tdd` |
56|| Debugging | `principle-fix-root-causes` |
57|| Finishing a task | `principle-prove-it-works` |
58|| Reviewing | `ponytail-review`, `interrogate`, `blast-radius` |
59|| Any prose: docs, UI copy, commit messages | `unslop`, `technical-writing` |
60|
61|If no row fits, read `.agents/skills/poteto-help/SKILL.md`, which maps situations to skills.

63|`interrogate` is written for Cursor. Under Muse, run the same review with Muse subagents and `muse-spark-1.3` as reviewers.
64|
65|## Workflow
66|
67|Each task follows the same loop. Muse Spark 1.3 Standard (`muse-spark-1.3`) writes the design in `docs/tasks/NN-name.md` and the review in `docs/reviews/NN.md`. `muse-spark-1.3-contributor` implements. Implement and review run at most two rounds.

73|## Lectoria rules
74|
75|- The text unit is the scene, not the paragraph or chapter.
76|- Paragraph ids are global, like `c12p34`.
77|- The emotion taxonomy has 8 ASCII ids: calma, alegria, tristeza, suspenso, misterio, aventura, combate, asombro. Jev returning `unknown` counts as low confidence and goes to the Muse override, which may return only the 8 ids. A hard failure stores no vector and the scene keeps the previous track. Never fake an emotion.
78|- Jev runs at `POST https://api.typesafe.ai/v1/systemone` with the model pinned to `jev-1.14.0`.
79|- Public-domain books only.
80|- Images follow the book text and the W. W. Denslow 1900 illustrations: silver shoes, nothing from the 1939 MGM film.
81|- Never copy code from github.com/martinmw13/lectoria.
82|- Test with the cheapest models (Contributor). Use Standard for the final pass and the public chat.
83|
84|## Product rules
85|
86|Owner decisions. Short and binding.
87|
88|- Desktop first. No mobile or iOS work now.
89|- The reader uses continuous scroll. The unit is the scene.
90|- A chapter holds several scenes. Each scene has its own emotion. Music changes at scene boundaries inside a chapter. No pagination.
91|- Reading position is the first paragraph visible at the top, tracked with IntersectionObserver.
92|- Paragraph ids carry a global ordinal `n`. Compare `n`, never id strings.
93|- `book.json` is frozen with a `textVersion` hash. Every cache key includes it.
94|- Scenes cover each chapter's paragraphs with no gaps and no overlaps. No scene crosses a chapter boundary.
95|- Emotions are distributions. Each scene stores the full Jev probability vector over the 8 ids, plus `intensity` (0 to 1) and `tempo` (energy, 0 to 1). The Muse override on low confidence edits the vector and records that it did. It never swaps in a single label.
96|- Music is about 15 tracks, pre-generated offline with MusicGen on Modal as one coherent soundtrack: same orchestra and instrumentation, same leitmotif style. Each track is a weighted blend of emotions and carries an emotion vector plus intensity and tempo. The proposed way to pick the blends: cluster the Oz scene vectors and use the centroids as track prompts.
97|- The player picks the track nearest to the scene vector, by cosine similarity over the vector plus intensity and tempo. Hysteresis stops it from flipping on small changes. Skip or change track overrides until the next scene.
98|- The owner listens to short clips before any full generation. Agents do not run Modal until the owner says so.
99|- MusicGen weights are CC-BY-NC. The hackathon demo is non-commercial. The generated tracks must say so in their README.
100|- Chat is low priority and simple. The context is the book text up to the reader's current position. The book prefix goes first and the question goes last, so readers share the prompt cache. Oz is about 55k tokens.
101|- The chat system prompt answers only from the provided text. It refuses knowledge beyond it, even if the model knows the book.
102|- A spoiler mode toggle is for readers who finished the book. It sends the whole text so they can ask about later events. No live Glimmer spoiler guard. No per-chapter summaries for chat. Citing passages is optional.
103|- Glimmer (open weights) keeps a pipeline role. Current decision: it writes the per-scene "why this music" explanation shown in the Developer View.
104|- Spikes come before feature code. Throwaway scripts in `scripts/spikes/` measure Muse Image (response format, latency, Denslow-style prompt), Meta `json_schema` structured output, and the Jev vector on a few Oz scenes. Results go to `docs/spikes.md`.
105|- Spend is counted in integer micro-dollars. Reserve with Redis `INCRBY` before each model call and refund with `DECRBY` after. Reserve per call, including retries.
106|- The server clamps every model tool argument. Tool arguments are untrusted input.
107|- The CSP allows `challenges.cloudflare.com` (script and frame) and `*.public.blob.vercel-storage.com` (images).
108|- The "Picture this" cache key is the paragraph range the selection touches (`firstPara..lastPara` ordinals) plus `textVersion` plus `promptVersion`. The prompt is built from those paragraphs.
109|- Images are cached only in Vercel Blob at deterministic paths (`addRandomSuffix: false`, check with `head()`). No Redis index. Routes return Blob URLs, never image bytes.
110|- Modal endpoints require proxy auth. Tokens live only in env.
111|
112|## Security rules
113|
114|Summary. The full rules live in [SECURITY.md](SECURITY.md).
115|
116|- Secrets live only in env vars: `.env.local` locally (gitignored), Vercel env vars in prod.
117|- `.env.example` holds names only, never values.
118|- Never use a `NEXT_PUBLIC_` variable for a secret. Only public ids such as the Turnstile site key may use it.
119|- `core/` stays pure: no keys, no env reads, no network clients, no `server-only`. Key-holding clients live in `server/` (Next.js only, each file starts with `import 'server-only'`) and in `pipeline/` (Node scripts that read env). Callers inject them into `core` functions as arguments. Tests run `core` with fake clients.
120|- The pre-commit secret scan must pass. Never bypass it with `--no-verify`.
121|- Errors to the client are generic. Details go to server logs only, never with keys.
122|- Never log request headers.
123|
124|## Writing rules
125|
126|Run docs, UI copy, and commit messages through the `unslop` skill: no filler, no hype, no emoji in headings, none of seamless, elevate, delve, robust, leverage. Headings use sentence case. Commit messages use an imperative subject under 72 chars, and the body says why.
127|
128|## Design
129|
130|Minimalist, functional, elegant. No generic AI-template look: no purple or violet anywhere, no gradient blobs, no glassmorphism, no emoji icons, no stock hero sections.
131|
132|The palette comes from Meta's brand. Meta blue `#0866FF` is the single accent, `#0064E0` for hover and pressed states. Text is near-black `#1C2B33`. Surfaces are white `#FFFFFF` and soft gray `#F1F4F7`. Dark mode keeps the same accent on a near-black surface: `#0B1215` surface, `#E4E6EB` text.
133|
134|The layout is typography-first. The book sits centered with a comfortable measure, about 60 to 70 chars per line. The companion chat lives in a quiet side panel. Whitespace is generous, the accent color is single, motion is subtle: under 200 ms, and it respects `prefers-reduced-motion`.
135|
136|These values live as CSS custom properties in [app/tokens.css](app/tokens.css), which is the source of truth.
137|
138|## Hooks
139|
140|`npm install` (or `npm run prepare`) points `core.hooksPath` at `.githooks`. The `pre-commit` hook rejects staged files over 5000 tokens and staged secrets. 11|Companion to `how` and `why`. `how` tells you what the code does. `why` tells you why it's shaped that way. Blast radius tells you what it breaks somewhere else.
12|
13|Listing the callers is not the job. The agent can grep those in a second. The job is the breakage grep won't show you.
14|
15|## Don't trust your own writeup
16|
17|A blast-radius writeup that sounds right is worthless. It reads as convincing whether or not it's true. So don't hand back the writeup. Find the one or two facts the whole thing depends on and prove them by running code.
18|
19|### How sure are you
20|
21|For each fact the change's safety depends on, get it as far down this list as is cheap, and say where it stopped.
22|
23|1. You said so. Worthless on its own.
24|2. You pointed at the line. A real `file:line`, or the library's own source.
25|3. You showed the bad case can't happen. You walked the failure step by step and it doesn't reach.
26|4. You ran it. A script or test that calls the real code and fails loud if you're wrong.

28|
29|Step 4 is usually one small script that imports the same library the app ships and calls the exact function you're worried about.
30|

32|
33|1. Read the change. The diff, the symbols it adds, changes, and deletes, and what it now does differently, including the part the diff doesn't spell out. Use `why` step 2 to pull the PR and commits.
34|2. Find the one fact it's safe because of. Most changes that look risky are safe because of a single fact, like "this call only drops already-dead cache entries and does nothing else". 9|
10|Apply the **type-system-discipline** principle skill first.
11|
12|| Rule | Summary |
13||------|---------|
14|| Discriminated unions | Model variants with a `kind` literal discriminant so impossible states can't be represented. No optional-field bags. |
15|| Branded types | Brand primitives with `& { readonly __brand: "X" }` so they can't be mixed up. Validate once at the boundary. A brand comes from a verifying type guard (`input is AgentId`), never from `as`. |
16|| Constructive modeling | Build the shape so the illegal value can't be constructed. `[T, ...T[]]` for non-empty, `[T, T][]` for even length, `start` plus `duration` for a range. Not a runtime guard, not a wish for refinement types. |
17|| Simplest total type | Keep `T[]` while every operation on it stays total. Strengthen to `NonEmpty<T>` only where the loose type forces `!`, a cast, or a "should never happen" throw. |
18|| `unknown` over `any` | External data is `unknown`. |
19|| Schemas before guards | Before hand-writing a property-by-property type guard, use the repository's runtime schema library and infer the type from the schema, such as `z.infer`. |
20|| No `as` casts | Every `as` is a runtime crash waiting. Cast only after validation. |
21|| Narrowing hierarchy | Discriminant switch > `in` operator > `typeof`/`instanceof` > user-defined type guard > `as`. |
22|| Type guards | Must verify the claim. A lying guard is worse than `as` because the bug hides behind a name that says it's safe. Name them `isX` or `hasX`. |
23|| Exhaustiveness | Inline `const _exhaustive: never = x;` in default arms so the compiler errors when a new variant is added. |
24|| `satisfies` over `as` | Validates the value without widening literal types. |
25|| Boundary validation | Parse where data crosses in, into a named domain type. `Record<string, unknown>` (however spelled) stops at that parse. Trust types inside. See the **boundary-discipline** principle skill. |
26|| Schema-derived types | Reach for `Pick`/`Omit`/`Parameters`/`ReturnType`/`Awaited`/`typeof` before declaring a new interface. |
27|| Object args | Pass objects, not positional, so argument order is self-documenting. Skip on hot paths (per-frame render, tokenizers, parsers). |
28|| Real tests | Don't mock what you can run. Prefer the framework's real test primitives with leak/disposable checks, and verify UI in a running build. Mock only what you can't run locally. |
29|| Structured telemetry | Prefer structured logger diagnostics with enough context to debug from an id. No `console.log` in shipped code. |
30|

8|# TypeScript best practices
9|
10|Apply the **type-system-discipline** principle skill first.
11|
12|| Rule | Summary |
13||------|---------|
14|| Discriminated unions | Model variants with a `kind` literal discriminant so impossible states can't be represented. No optional-field bags. |
15|| Branded types | Brand primitives with `& { readonly __brand: "X" }` so they can't be mixed up. Validate once at the boundary. A brand comes from a verifying type guard (`input is AgentId`), never from `as`. |
16|| Constructive modeling | Build the shape so the illegal value can't be constructed. `[T, ...T[]]` for non-empty, `[T, T][]` for even length, `start` plus `duration` for a range. Not a runtime guard, not a wish for refinement types. |
17|| Simplest total type | Keep `T[]` while every operation on it stays total. Strengthen to `NonEmpty<T>` only where the loose type forces `!`, a cast, or a "should never happen" throw. |
18|| `unknown` over `any` | External data is `unknown`. |
19|| Schemas before guards | Before hand-writing a property-by-property type guard, use the repository's runtime schema library and infer the type from the schema, such as `z.infer`. |
20|| No `as` casts | Every `as` is a runtime crash waiting. Cast only after validation. |
21|| Narrowing hierarchy | Discriminant switch > `in` operator > `typeof`/`instanceof` > user-defined type guard > `as`. |
22|| Type guards | Must verify the claim. A lying guard is worse than `as` because the bug hides behind a name that says it's safe. Name them `isX` or `hasX`. |
23|| Exhaustiveness | Inline `const _exhaustive: never = x;` in default arms so the compiler errors when a new variant is added. |
24|| `satisfies` over `as` | Validates the value without widening literal types. |
25|| Boundary validation | Parse where data crosses in, into a named domain type. `Record<string, unknown>` (however spelled) stops at that parse. Trust types inside. See the **boundary-discipline** principle skill. |
26|| Schema-derived types | Reach for `Pick`/`Omit`/`Parameters`/`ReturnType`/`Awaited`/`typeof` before declaring a new interface. |
27|| Object args | Pass objects, not positional, so argument order is self-documenting. Skip on hot paths (per-frame render, tokenizers, parsers). |
28|| Real tests | Don't mock what you can run. Prefer the framework's real test primitives with leak/disposable checks, and verify UI in a running build. Mock only what you can't run locally. |
29|| Structured telemetry | Prefer structured logger diagnostics with enough context to debug from an id. No `console.log` in shipped code. |

7|# Blast radius
8|
9|Find what a change breaks somewhere else, before it ships. Use for "blast radius of X", "what could this break", or reviewing a small diff you don't trust yet.
10|
11|Companion to `how` and `why`. `how` tells you what the code does. `why` tells you why it's shaped that way. Blast radius tells you what it breaks somewhere else.
12|
13|Listing the callers is not the job. The agent can grep those in a second. The job is the breakage grep won't show you.
14|
15|## Don't trust your own writeup
16|
17|A blast-radius writeup that sounds right is worthless. It reads as convincing whether or not it's true. So don't hand back the writeup. Find the one or two facts the whole thing depends on and prove them by running code.
18|
19|### How sure are you
20|
21|For each fact the change's safety depends on, get it as far down this list as is cheap, and say where it stopped.
22|
23|1. You said so. Worthless on its own.
24|2. You pointed at the line. A real `file:line`, or the library's own source.
25|3. You showed the bad case can't happen. You walked the failure step by step and it doesn't reach.
26|4. You ran it. A script or test that calls the real code and fails loud if you're wrong.
27|5. You reproduced it in the running app.
28|
29|Step 4 is usually one small script that imports the same library the app ships and calls the exact function you're worried about.
30|
31|## Steps
32|
33|1. Read the change. The diff, the symbols it adds, changes, and deletes, and what it now does differently, including the part the diff doesn't spell out. Use `why` step 2 to pull the PR and commits.
34|2. Find the one fact it's safe because of. Most changes that look risky are safe because of a single fact, like "this call only drops already-dead cache entries and does nothing else". Find that fact. If it holds, most risky cases are cleared at once. Spend your time here, not on a long list of maybes.
35|3. Look where grep stops. Read the source of the library you call, and check its pinned version and any local patch. Work out when things run: microtasks, unmount and teardown, Solid versus React. Follow what a symbol search misses: the JSON an API returns, a DB column, a wire format, another language reading the same bytes, a feature flag, code three hops downstream.
36|4. Be honest about each risk. Give it a real chance of happening and a real cost if it does. Keep the risks you confirmed. List the ones you checked and cleared separately. Same rules as `why`. Cite a real `file:line`, a search that finds nothing is still an answer, and never make up a caller or an API.
37|5. Prove the one fact. Write a script or test that runs the real code, run it, and paste what happened.
38|6. For a big or wide change, run it as an `arena`. Ask more than one model the same question and merge the answers. Different models catch different real bugs.
39|
40|## What to hand back
41|
42|- **What it does.** What changed, including the part that isn't obvious.
43|- **The one fact it's safe because of.** State it, say which step you got it to, and show the proof. If you couldn't prove it, write unproven.
44|- **Risks.** Each names how it breaks, the `file:line`, how likely and how bad, and how to check. Paste the proof for the ones that matter.
45|- **Cleared.** What you checked and why it's fine.
46|- **Before you merge.** The cheapest test or repro that catches the real bug, including the script you wrote.
47|
48|Write it through `unslop`, cite real code, and strip anything private before it goes anywhere public.
49|
50|**Reply:** the writeup above, with the one safety fact either proven or marked unproven.

1|# Contracts
2|
3|Music generation must never block the reader. Each module below owns one
4|job and can be swapped without touching the others. Import direction is
5|`core <- server` and `core <- app`. Server and client components never
6|import each other. `app/page.tsx` may import `server/books.ts`. Client
7|files never do.
8|
9|## Book data
10|
11|`data/books/oz/book.json` holds the frozen text: id, title, author,
12|`textVersion` hash, chapters with `start_n` and `end_n`, and paragraphs
13|with `id`, `ch`, `n`, and `text`. `scenes.json` holds scene ranges and
14|titles. `analysis.json` holds the same scenes plus Jev vectors, the Muse
15|override, and the `final` emotion. The reader consumes the book fields,
16|scene ranges and titles, and the `final` vector with intensity and tempo.
17|It never sees `jev`, `muse_override`, or provenance. `core/reader.ts`
18|defines `buildReaderModel`, which joins paragraphs to scenes by ordinal
19|range and throws on unordered scenes or on paragraphs covered zero or
20|two times.
21|
22|## Music library
23|
24|The library is a static `public/music/manifest.json`, fetched by the
25|client from `/music/manifest.json`. A static file needs no route, ships
26|from the CDN, and swaps by replacing files plus a version bump. Shape:
27|
28|`MusicManifest = { version, tracks }`. `Track = { id, src, label,
29|vector, intensity, tempo, durationSec, loop }`. The vector covers the 8
30|emotion ids in `core/types.ts`. `core/music.ts` owns `parseManifest`,
31|which rejects unknown versions, missing fields, bad vectors, numbers
32|outside 0..1, and any `src` that is not a `/music/` path or `https` URL.
33|The reader calls it on every fetch, so a bad drop-in fails loudly in
34|dev. Remote URLs need a `media-src` addition in `next.config.ts`.
35|
36|## Track selection
37|
38|`selectTrack(scene, manifest, currentTrackId, opts)` in `core/music.ts`
39|is pure. It scores cosine similarity over `buildFeatures` from
40|`core/cluster.ts` (vector plus weighted intensity and tempo) and keeps
41|the current track unless the best beats it by `margin` (default 0.05),
42|which stops flicker between nearby scenes. A null scene means a hard
43|failure with no vector, so it holds the current track and returns null
44|with no current track. An empty manifest returns null. Ties follow
45|manifest order. `nextAlternative(scene, manifest, currentTrackId)` ranks
46|the same way and returns the next track after the current one, wrapping
47|around, so repeated presses cycle through every track. One track returns
48|itself. A skip overrides until the next scene: the reader holds the
49|override per scene and reruns selection on scene change with the
50|override track as current.
51|
52|## Player
53|
54|`app/player.tsx` takes a track or null plus the scene title and an
55|`onSkip` callback. It owns two `audio` elements, play state, volume, and
56|the 1.5 s crossfade on change (0 when the user prefers reduced motion).
57|Loop stays on. Audio starts only after the user presses play. On manifest
58|failure the reader still renders and the bar shows a short neutral note.
59|UI motion stays under 200 ms. Controls are real buttons and inputs with
60|labels, visible focus, and keyboard use.
61|
62|## Image api
63|
64|Contract only, no routes. Request `{ bookId, textVersion, firstN, lastN
65|}` names the selection by touched paragraph ordinals. Response `{ url }`
66|is a Vercel Blob URL. The cache key is `firstN..lastN` plus
67|`textVersion` plus `promptVersion` at a deterministic Blob path with
68|`addRandomSuffix: false`. The server checks the path with `head()`
69|before generating and never returns bytes. The same paragraph range
70|reuses the image. Types live in `core/types.ts`.
71|
72|## Chat api
73|
74|Contract only, no routes. Request `{ bookId, textVersion, positionN,
75|spoilerMode, messages }` carries the chat history and the reader
76|position. The response is streamed text. The server builds context from
77|the book text up to `positionN`, or the whole book when `spoilerMode` is
78|on, with the book prefix first and the question last so readers share
79|the prompt cache. The system prompt answers only from that text and
80|refuses the rest. Types live in `core/types.ts`.
81|
82|## Quotas and budget
83|
84|Server only. Spend is counted in integer micro-dollars: reserve with
85|Redis `INCRBY` before each model call, refund with `DECRBY` after, one
86|reserve per call including retries. The server clamps every model tool
87|argument. Clients never see keys or raw errors. Generic messages go to
88|the client, details stay in server logs.
